passage: I was on the compound wall eating peanuts when it happened. Yash, from Class 8, stood with two other big boys near the water tank. Little Santosh from Class 5 held a piece of a broken flowerpot and looked as if he might cry. "Just bury it under the bush and say nothing," said Yash. "Or you will be the one who broke it." Santosh looked at the bush, then at the staff room, then at the ground. The other two big boys watched. I could not tell what Santosh would do; his hand shook. After the bell I told our class teacher what I had seen, and she went to the tank straight away.

qa.q: Where did Yash tell Santosh to bury the piece of flowerpot?
qa.a: Yash told Santosh to bury it under the bush and say nothing.

qa.q: What might Santosh be feeling as looking from the bush to the staff room to the ground?
qa.a: Santosh seems torn and frightened: pulled to obey an older boy, yet with a sinking sense that hiding the piece is wrong.

qa.q: What choice by the narrator helped after the bell?
qa.a: The narrator told the class teacher what had been seen, and the teacher went to the water tank straight away.

qa.q: Why might the two other big boys stay silent while Yash speaks?
qa.a: They may fear that speaking against Yash would make them the next target, or may be following along to belong; the passage shows only that they watch.

grounding: A child is told by an older student to hide something and keep a secret, feeling the pull between obedience and a sense of wrongness.

passage: Monday. On the school bus Dhruv from Class 8 leaned over. "Put Eshaan's bottle in your bag, Alka. Do not tell." Alka laughed as if it were a joke, then did it. Her stomach sank. Tuesday. Eshaan searched under every seat with pink eyes, and Alka could not swallow her lunch. Dhruv winked at her. Wednesday. In the corridor Alka gave the bottle back and told the class teacher what Dhruv had said. The teacher sat beside her, said she had done the right thing and it was not her fault, and took Dhruv and Eshaan to the head that same afternoon.

qa.q: What did Dhruv tell Alka to put in her bag?
qa.a: Dhruv told Alka to put Eshaan's bottle in her bag and not tell.

qa.q: How did Alka feel on Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: Alka felt guilty and uneasy: a sinking stomach and not being able to swallow lunch show the pull between obeying an older boy and knowing it was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: Alka gave the bottle back and told the class teacher, who stayed with Alka, said it was not Alka's fault, and took the matter to the head that afternoon.

qa.q: What might Tuesday have been like for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan searched under every seat with pink eyes, which suggests worry and upset over the missing bottle, and no idea who could be responsible.

grounding: A child is told by an older student to hide something and keep quiet, feeling a stomach-sinking wrongness across three days.

passage:
Jaya, you want to hear about Nani's schooldays? Alright. This is your Zainab nani talking, and I'll tell it straight.
In Class 6 there was a senior girl, Farhana, a prefect with a badge. One day she handed me a new girl's pencil box. “Hide this in your desk. It's a joke. Don't tell anyone, or else.”
I held it and my stomach dropped like a stone. Prefects were like teachers to us. But the new girl was searching everywhere, almost crying.
I lasted till the last bell. Then I walked to the class teacher and gave her the box and told her who gave it. She thanked me, found Farhana that same afternoon, and made her apologise. I shook all the way home.

qa.q: What did Farhana hand young Zainab?
qa.a: She handed her a new girl's pencil box.

qa.q: How did young Zainab feel while holding the pencil box?
qa.a: She felt torn and sick with guilt; her stomach dropped, pulled between obeying a prefect and seeing the new girl nearly cry.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things?
qa.a: At the last bell, Zainab chose to give the box to the class teacher and say who gave it, and the teacher dealt with it that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might the new girl have felt during the search?
qa.a: She was likely frightened and upset, searching everywhere and almost crying, possibly feeling unwelcome in a new class.

grounding: An elder recalls being told by an older student to hide something and keep it secret, feeling a pull between obedience and a sense of wrongness.

passage:
The cricket ball had cracked the big flowerpot outside the staffroom, and the bell for assembly would ring in two minutes.
Nilesh, a Class 8 monitor, pushed the ball into Uday's hands. “Put it in your bag. You're small, nobody will check you. Don't say anything.” The other seniors scattered.
Uday stood with the ball in his hands. Nilesh was a monitor. Monitors were obeyed. But his stomach felt like it was sinking through his shoes. Mrs Joshi would think the pot fell by itself.
The bell rang. Uday walked into the staffroom instead of assembly. “Ma'am, this broke the pot. I didn't throw it.” Mrs Joshi put down her tea, thanked him for telling her, and sent for Nilesh before assembly ended.

qa.q: What had the cricket ball cracked?
qa.a: It had cracked the big flowerpot outside the staffroom.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling as he stood holding the ball?
qa.a: He felt torn and sick with worry; his stomach felt like it was sinking because hiding it felt wrong even though a monitor ordered it.

qa.q: How did Mrs Joshi handle Uday's news, and why did it help?
qa.a: She stopped, thanked him for telling her and sent for Nilesh at once, so Uday knew he had done right and wasn't left to face the seniors alone.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nilesh when he's called in?
qa.a: He may feel caught and embarrassed, and maybe angry with Uday, which is why the teacher's quick support for Uday matters.

grounding: Shows a child told by an older student to hide something and keep quiet, feeling the pull between obedience and a sinking sense of wrongness.

passage:
On the school van, Yamini didi ruled the back seat. She was in Class 7 and everyone listened to her.
A new girl got on with a pink bag and sat near the window. Yamini leaned over to Devika. “Tell her she can't sit here. Go on. Say it.”
Two other girls giggled. Devika looked at the new girl, who was holding her bag tightly on her lap. Something in Devika's stomach sank.
“Say it,” Yamini repeated.
Devika opened her mouth. “Um. That's... that's didi's side,” she mumbled.
The new girl moved to the front without a word. Yamini patted Devika's head. All the way to school, Devika stared at the back of the new girl's pink bag and felt sick.

qa.q: Who ruled the back seat of the van?
qa.a: Yamini didi ruled the back seat.

qa.q: How did Devika feel after the new girl moved?
qa.a: She felt sick and guilty, staring at the pink bag, even though Yamini patted her head.

qa.q: What could Devika do tomorrow to put things right?
qa.a: She could sit with the new girl or say sorry, and tell the van aunty or a teacher if Yamini keeps pushing people out.

qa.q: What was the van ride like for the new girl?
qa.a: She likely felt unwelcome and alone, moving to the front silently and holding her bag tightly.

grounding: Shows a child told by an older student to pick on a newcomer, obeying while feeling a stomach-sinking sense of wrongness.

passage:
"Pooja. Come here." Abhinav from Class 7 leaned on the railing, Sunny grinning beside him. "Kiran's tiffin is in the blue bag. Hide it behind the water tank before lunch."
"Why?"
"Because I'm telling you. Seniors' orders." Sunny laughed. "And not a word to anyone."
Pooja's stomach dropped. "Kiran didn't do anything."
"So? It's a joke."
At the lunch bell Pooja stood by the blue bag, hand hovering. Then she walked to the staffroom.
"Ma'am, a senior told me to hide Kiran's tiffin and not tell."
Ms D'Souza put down her pen. "Thank you for telling me. You did nothing wrong. Stay with me while I make sure Kiran has lunch, and I'll speak to Abhinav's class teacher before home time today."

qa.q: Where did Abhinav tell Pooja to hide Kiran's tiffin?
qa.a: Behind the water tank, before lunch.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling as she stood by the blue bag with her hand hovering?
qa.a: Pooja felt torn and scared: a senior's order pulled one way, while a sinking feeling said it was wrong to hurt Kiran.

qa.q: What did Ms D'Souza's response get right?
qa.a: Ms D'Souza thanked Pooja, said Pooja did nothing wrong, kept Pooja close, looked after Kiran and acted on it the same day.

qa.q: What would have changed for Kiran if Pooja had obeyed?
qa.a: Kiran would have lost lunch and felt picked on for no reason, probably without ever knowing who did it.

grounding: Shows a child told by an older student to pick on a classmate and keep it secret, feeling the pull between obeying and a sense of wrongness.
